WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : The United States on Wednesday banned imports from three Chinese genomics companies for allegedly working with the government of Xinjiang to enable the forced labor of Uyghur and other ethnic minorities. The companies are BGI Genomics Co.. Ltd, (300676.SZ), MGI Tech Co Ltd. (688114.SS) and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co Ltd, which the U.S. says is also known as the BGI Group. The companies were added to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which identifies entities that use or facilitate the use of forced labor of Uyghurs and other minorities, or source material from the Xinjiang region. Beijing has regularly dismissed accusations of forced labor and other abuses against Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in the Xinjiang region

Oct 28 : Telenor's efforts to persuade mobile customers to pay more for network quality and security services could face a new test from AI shopping agents expected to focus heavily on price, executives said on Wednesday. The Norwegian operator's "more-for-more" strategy adds benefits to subscriptions to encourage higher spending. Its task is to make those extras count when customers compare offers. AI agents would be "to a large degree price driven", CEO Benedicte Schilbred Fasmer told Reuters, saying the benefits beyond connectivity needed to be clear to customers. That would add another dimension to an already competitive market. Telenor lost 22,000 mobile subscriptions in Norway in the third quarter, while mobile revenue per user rose 2.7 per cent year on year.

Oct 28 : Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase is adding Ripple's stablecoin RLUSD to its platform, expanding its slate of dollar-backed crypto tokens.  The move is a boost for blockchain payments company Ripple, which launched RLUSD in December 2024 to facilitate near-instant settlement of cross-border payments. The stablecoin has a market capitalization of more than $2.5 billion, according to data provider CoinGecko.  RLUSD will be available starting Wednesday across Coinbase's retail and institutional platforms, Coinbase said. For years, Circle's USDC was the flagship stablecoin Coinbase offered to its customers, but Coinbase has gradually expanded its stablecoin offerings to include PayPal's PYUSD, as well as Open USD, a stablecoin issued through a joint venture backed by Visa, Mastercard and Coinbase.   "It's a really credentializing moment for RLUSD to not only be listed on Coinbase but to be embraced across the platform," said Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple.  Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to keep a constant value and backed by traditional currencies, most commonly the US dollar. They are used mainly to trade in and out of other cryptocurrencies, such as bitcoin, but proponents say they can also facilitate instant payments and corporate treasury management.

LOS ANGELES, Oct 28 : Apple is expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBooks on Wednesday, abandoning a long-held aversion to the technology as it caps a burst of product launches ahead of the crucial holiday shopping season. Apple is holding an event in Los Angeles after launching a folding iPhone, Duo, at its Silicon Valley headquarters in September and a smart home hub in New York earlier this month. While those products will test new markets for Apple, the Los Angeles event could rekindle an old question: should Apple put the touchscreens that it made mainstream in iPhones and iPads in its oldest product line? Apple executives long resisted the idea, with Steve Jobs saying in 2010 that touchscreens on laptops were "ergonomically terrible" and then-CEO Tim Cook saying in 2012 that such devices would be as pleasing to users as converging a toaster and a refrigerator. Before becoming Apple's current CEO, John Ternus argued that Apple already made a touchscreen computer with its iPad lineup. But touchscreens have been widely available for more than a decade on Windows devices, and with the iPhone nearing its two-decade anniversary, a new generation of buyers expects screens to respond to touch.

LONDON/HONG KONG, Oct 28 : With jet fuel prices at roughly double their levels before the Iran war, airlines are growing increasingly reluctant to lock in future fuel costs through new hedges, warning instead of steep fare increases to offset higher fuel bills. Hedging allows airlines to lock in future fuel prices, helping shield them from increases and providing greater certainty over costs. But some programmes require premiums, collateral or other costs, while airlines that hedge at current elevated prices risk being locked into expensive fuel if geopolitical tensions ease and prices retreat. As the conflict in the Middle East enters its ninth month, the strategy shift means fliers globally will likely pay far higher air fares as carriers lose their hedging protection, testing consumer willingness to shell out more for travel. "Most hedging is finishing," AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes told Reuters this month, adding the Malaysian airline was budgeting for 12 months of high oil prices and had "given up trying to predict" how geopolitical tensions would evolve.

He said the firm was not even modelling a scenario where oil prices fall. "So everyone's going to be exposed. There's only one way or two ways of dealing with that: cut costs or raise fares." Finland's Finnair, which said this month that high fuel costs had fed through to ticket prices, has stopped adding new hedges as fuel costs surged this year. It has an average hedging ratio of 34 per cent for 2027. "With such high prices, how do you then lock in low prices again?" finance chief Pia Aaltonen-Forsell said on Tuesday. "If we add right now, it's more expensive." NO EUROPEAN AIRLINE WELL HEDGED THROUGH 2027, RYANAIR SAYS Jet fuel accounts for between 30 per cent and 40 per cent of airlines' costs, with European and Asian carriers historically hedging more of their fuel needs than US rivals, which largely abandoned the practice after costly bets on oil prices backfired. "You have stability of cost when you hedge," said Jeffrey Goh, managing director at Alton Aviation, adding it remained a bet on prices rising — and could backfire. "You have to look at the forward curve and predict how fast it might go down." The pressure could intensify in 2027 as hedges put in place before the war expire, exposing airlines more fully to current fuel prices. "None of the European airlines, including Ryanair, are well-hedged until summer of 2027, so I think you're going to have to see air fares rise by 15 per cent to 20 per cent," Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary told reporters earlier this month. Ryanair said in September it had stopped hedging. Europe's largest airline has hedged about 80 per cent of its jet fuel needs for the year ending March 2027. In a sign of challenges airlines may face pushing higher fares, budget carrier Norwegian Air Shuttle said on Wednesday it had been forced to undo some post-Iran war price hikes because customers "were not willing to pay". FUEL HEDGING NOT A 'COMPLETE SOLUTION' Globally, airline hedging policies remain fragmented, with some carriers expanding programmes since the war began and others dialling them back. Carriers with weak balance sheets also often have less flexibility to absorb the costs associated with hedging and can be fully exposed to fuel-price movements, contributing to a flurry of recent bankruptcy and insolvency filings. US airlines have largely shown little appetite to return to hedging despite this year's fuel shock. Analysts say US consumers tend to be less price sensitive than travellers in other regions and the most willing to absorb higher fares. Air fares in the European Union rose 5.8 per cent year-on-year in September, the latest official data show. US air fares, meanwhile, were up more than 20 per cent year-on-year in the month. American, United, Delta, JetBlue and Allegiant have no material fuel hedges, while Frontier has no active hedging position. Southwest ended its long-running programme last year, while Alaska and Hawaiian also closed out remaining positions. The reluctance of some European and Asian airlines to add new hedges could signal a broader shift in industry attitudes towards fuel hedging, although this year's fuel-price spike has also highlighted the risks of remaining exposed to fuel markets. Delta, United and Southwest all cut profit targets or disappointed investors with their earnings outlooks this month as fuel expenses climbed. Despite hedging more than 70 per cent of their jet fuel needs for this year, Ryanair and Lufthansa cut capacity on some routes to limit the impact of unhedged fuel costs. "Fuel remains the single largest area of uncertainty in the outlook," said Air New Zealand Chief Financial Officer Kris Cudmore. "Our hedging program provides some nearer term protection, but it is far from a complete solution."

Oct 28 : The US dollar held onto gains on Wednesday after reaching a two-week high ahead of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, while sterling investors awaited the Andy Burnham government's first budget, hoping it would avoid a heavy reliance on borrowing. The week is packed with monetary policy decisions by central banks globally as policymakers weigh the path ahead for interest rates against the backdrop of price pressures due to the Middle East conflict and ballooning sovereign debt costs. Traders broadly expect no change in Fed monetary policy after a series of Fed officials in recent weeks signalled the need to wait and watch for more signs of persistent price pressures. However, they see a 78 per cent chance that the central bank could lift interest rates by at least 25 basis points in December, the CME Group's FedWatch tool showed. The euro was flat at $1.1126, trading just above the May 2025 low it hit earlier this month, while against the yen, the dollar was steady at 157.89 yen.

The pound slipped 0.1 per cent to $1.328 and was about 0.2 per cent lower versus the euro, but sterling was close to the 17-month high versus the euro hit in the previous session. Investors will be keen to see how the government expects to raise revenue, with analysts expecting taxes on banks, gambling firms and online marketplaces. "The expectation is that the UK is maybe a little bit more fiscally constrained than many of its European peers. So if the government doesn't do anything too negative, there's room for the market to be somewhat pleasantly surprised in this," said Michael Leithead, head of fixed income at EFG Asset Management. However, given the recent scrutiny around government debt, any significant reliance on borrowing could spark a selloff in the currency and gilts.  CANADIAN RATE HIKE AWAITED; KIWI FALLS Later in the day, the Canadian central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by at least 25 basis points in a preemptive move to stop energy-led inflation from spreading into the rest of the economy.  The Canadian dollar inched up 0.1 per cent to C$1.403 per US dollar.  The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are also expected to deliver monetary policy verdicts on Thursday and Friday, respectively, with both central banks expected to leave policy rates unchanged.    The New Zealand dollar sank as much as 1.3 per cent to $0.5609 after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand held interest rates at 2.75 per cent, surprising a large majority of economists who had expected a rate hike. Oct 28 : In the AI capital of the world, sixth-grade humanities teacher Tristen Chang is designing her classroom so students can’t rely on chatbots. Starting last year, Chang did away with take-home essays and began using oral exams to test students at her San Francisco school. She asks students 15 questions about character, plot, theme and metaphor, which they can answer in as little as five minutes. "There’s been a long march of technology changing teaching, but AI is the most drastic," Chang said. "Everything’s out the window.” As generative AI becomes ubiquitous, US middle and high school teachers are rethinking how they assess learning. Educators are assigning less take-home work, increasing in-class writing and discussion, and redesigning assignments to measure students' thinking rather than simply their answers, according to Reuters interviews with a dozen teachers and education experts across the country.

School systems remain divided over AI, leaving many teachers to navigate the transition largely on their own. Some want AI integrated into classrooms; others want it restricted. Many occupy a middle ground. “Where many adults are using these tools for various kinds of purposes to help them in work-based settings, we haven't really figured out what that means for education,” said Antero Garcia, an education professor at Stanford University and president of the National Council of Teachers of English. A FIXTURE IN EDUCATION As students gain access to AI chatbots on their phones and laptops, teachers are moving more learning back into the classroom. They are increasingly relying on in-class writing, instruction and face-to-face assessment.  Rusty Shabe, who teaches middle school English in San Francisco, said students often turn to AI at home when they feel overwhelmed. He is trying to combat that impulse by devoting more classroom time to writing, taking a month, for example, to work on an essay with seventh-graders.  Bobson Wong, a high school math teacher in New York, now assigns fewer homework questions and more in-class practice so he can better monitor how his students are working. “AI has definitely changed not just how students do math, but how I teach it,” Wong said.  AI's effect on learning is up for debate. A 2025 Harvard randomized trial found that a custom AI tutor improved learning gains and student engagement, while a small 2025 MIT Media Lab study found that people who used ChatGPT to write essays did the work faster, but appeared to do less thinking. Even so, AI is becoming a fixture in education: a 2025 RAND survey found that the majority of US students and English, math and science teachers reported using AI for schoolwork. Last spring, Meghan Hyland, a high school English teacher in a New York City suburb, realized some students were heading to the bathroom to access AI on their phones. Although phones were already banned in her class, she began requiring students to leave them behind when they left.  She has also made classwork a bigger component of students' grades and stopped relying on homework as practice.   “My main ability to understand whether they know how to do critical thinking has to be done in school,” Hyland said. For some educators, the best way to beat AI is to avoid predictable questions. Because AI is adept at answering conventional questions about character and plot, some teachers have begun asking students for interpretations that depart from mainstream thinking.  “I try very hard to create prompts that, at the moment at least, AI is imperfect at responding to,” said Pian Rockfeld, a high school English teacher in the Bronx.  Among her other strategies: assigning essays that require students to read scholarly articles that typically sit behind a paywall, protected from AI chatbots.  ‘YOU CAN’T HIDE WHEN THE LAPTOPS ARE AWAY’ For some teachers, AI is accelerating a broader backlash against classroom technology, motivating them to move away from screens and toward notebooks, pen-and-paper writing and physical projects. Rex Ovalle, a high school English teacher in a Chicago suburb, tells students to retrieve a composition notebook from a box at the start of class. He limits Chromebook use to roughly 10 per cent of school days. “I have seen a lot of engagement because you can’t hide when the laptops are away,” Ovalle said. While Chromebooks and other technology became pervasive during the COVID-19 pandemic, many school districts are now re-evaluating their technology use amid concerns about excessive screen time. In Hyland’s English classes, students write by hand except when they require special accommodations. She has developed new ways to assess their comprehension of a book, such as assigning a cooking demonstration to show how they understand “A Tale of Two Cities." A black-and-white cookie, for example, represented the book's famous opening line about the best of times and worst of times. Hyland said she looks for lessons that involve “something done live so that in real time they are showing creative thinking.” Even as they worry about misuse, some teachers are embracing AI as a classroom tool. They said it can help them find articles on a specific topic, design classroom signage and develop graphics for slide presentations, for example. Michael Zagari, a high school social studies teacher in a New York City suburb, uses AI to change the vocabulary in historical documents for students at different reading levels and to condense articles so he can cover them in class. He encourages students to use AI to get started on research projects and thinks they develop critical thinking skills by learning how to effectively prompt AI. “AI is not going away,” Zagari said. “We need to teach civic responsibility of how to use AI just like we taught responsible use of the Internet.”

Oct 28 : Two teenage plaintiffs who say social media caused them to develop serious mental health problems will take Meta Platforms and Snap to trial in Los Angeles on Wednesday in the latest test of claims raised in thousands of US lawsuits over social media's impact on young people. The case is only the second to go to trial involving individual plaintiffs who allege that social media companies deliberately designed their platforms to be addictive. Social media companies lost the first such trial to the tune of $6 million in damages in March. Plaintiffs referred to in court papers as S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi, have said they began using YouTube as early as age 3 or 4 and other platforms around age 9. They have alleged that autoplay, infinite scroll and other features drove them to compulsive use, and they developed depression, anxiety and eating disorders as a result. The trial, which begins with the jury selection process on Wednesday, is expected to run for several weeks. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram head Adam Mosseri and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel are expected to testify.

The two plaintiffs initially sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube, in addition to Meta and Snap. Both reached settlements with TikTok and YouTube ahead of trial, and the Illinois plaintiff also settled with Meta. Wednesday's trial covers claims by both plaintiffs against Snap, and the Mississippi plaintiff's claims against Meta. Meta and Snap have asked Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn Kuhl, presiding over the proceedings, to split the cases into separate trials, arguing that trying them together would unfairly mix up the evidence for jurors. The judge has not yet ruled on that request. 'A YOUNG PERSON'S MENTAL HEALTH' A Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with the claims made against it and has built protections into its platforms for a decade. Meta owns Instagram and Facebook. "A young person's mental health is shaped by many factors, as the evidence in this trial will show," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The plaintiff used TikTok far more than Instagram or Facebook, and her personal circumstances were a substantial factor in her struggles." A Snap spokesperson said its Snapchat platform is different from traditional social media because it does not open to a feed or a ranking of what other people post. The company has built safeguards into its platform, the spokesperson said. "We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent their experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed," the spokesperson said. Emily Jeffcott, an attorney representing the Mississippi plaintiff, said in a statement ahead of the trial that "we look forward to educating the jury about the dangers of features like endless feeds, autoplay and streaks and how Meta – and allegedly Snap as well – have implemented and emphasized these features."  A TEST CASE Plaintiffs S.J. and K.D.B. sued in 2023. Both described staying awake for hours scrolling social media, losing focus in class and engaging in self-harm using methods shown in social media videos. They are seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages. Their cases are among more than 3,000 lawsuits brought by individuals and others that have been consolidated in Los Angeles Superior Court. Their lawsuits have been selected as bellwethers, or test cases, meaning the verdict could influence how the companies and plaintiffs resolve the remaining cases. Social media companies have denied that their platforms were designed to addict young people, and have said they have taken action to make the apps safe for young users. They also have argued that they are shielded from the claims by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 1996 federal law that generally protects online platforms from liability over user-generated content.  The trial judge disagreed that Section 230 bars claims over how the sites are designed, and allowed the suits by the two plaintiffs to go to trial.  In the case decided in March, a Los Angeles jury found that Meta and YouTube were negligent, siding with a young woman referred to in court papers as Kaley G.M. There have been multiple cases scheduled for trial since then, but the companies have settled the claims or, in some cases, the plaintiffs have chosen to drop them. SCHOOL DISTRICTS AND STATES SUE More than 3,800 lawsuits brought by states, school districts and individuals over similar claims are pending in federal court in California, court records showed. In August, Meta reached settlements worth up to $18 billion to resolve claims made by nearly every US state and territory over the impact of its platforms on teen mental health. The company agreed as part of that deal to change how teens can access Instagram and Facebook. Members of Meta's senior legal team told reporters after that settlement that the company views the individual and school district cases as harder to prove at trial than cases brought by states because they require plaintiffs to directly link specific problems to its social media platforms. Meta is appealing the verdict in the case decided in March, arguing that Section 230 should have barred the claims by plaintiff Kaley G.M. A ruling in Meta's favor on the issue could derail thousands of lawsuits over youth mental health and shield it from billions of dollars in potential liability that the company has said poses a serious threat to its future, according to experts.

Oct 28 : On more than 100,000 acres of Nevada desert east of Reno, one of the world's largest concentrations of data centers is taking shape, providing years of work for thousands of electricians, pipefitters and other union tradespeople who are building it. About 400 miles southeast, along the iconic Las Vegas Strip, the AI technology powered by such data centers is taking a toll: Self-driving Zoox and Waymos are replacing human-driven taxis and valets; casino floor bartenders are being replaced by robots; and MGM's massive call center is slashing hundreds of jobs. That split screen is challenging the Nevada Teamsters, a politically powerful network of local labor unions representing 30,000 workers across the construction, transportation and hospitality industries, many of whom will be voting in the Nov. 3 elections. Some want to see new data-center construction halted or slowed. Others view the boom as a gift. "My job is to represent all of our unions," said Ross Kinson, the Nevada Teamsters’ political director, adding the group had launched a process in April to find a unified stance ahead of the November polls.

"This is a very, very important issue to the building trades, and it's providing a lot of jobs and creating good opportunities for a lot of people." But, he said, he has been encouraging members to consider the flip side: "What is it doing to our jobs?" Nevada unions’ soul-searching reflects the national debate underway over whether regulation should slow down AI development amid conflicting projections of job destruction and creation – and whether AI will ultimately lift humanity or harm it. It’s likely to affect Nevada's voting on Nov. 3. The Nevada Teamsters interviewed more than 180 political candidates from both parties ahead of the election, Kinson said. Those who didn’t support strong worker protections, or those looking for an outright ban on new data-center construction, were unlikely to win the union's backing.   "It's a political minefield for politicians to tiptoe through," said Kinson.   Nevada will also play a significant role in the 2028 presidential elections as the second state in the Democratic primary schedule behind South Carolina.   ROBOT BARTENDERS On a suburban street just off the Las Vegas Strip, 63-year-old Larry Goldfinger and a group of fellow Teamsters he jokingly calls "the walking dead" trudge through the desert heat, clipboards in hand. They’re knocking on doors to promote candidates they believe will protect the city’s workers from AI-driven job losses. Goldfinger has spent nearly three decades as a valet at some of the Strip's most iconic casinos, and another decade in Vegas hospitality jobs – work he now fears will dry up as AI automation takes over everything from concierge services to bartending.  "I raised my family, and I have had a good life doing it, and I feel like these guys that are 30ish aren't going to be able to do that," he said, wearing a Teamsters baseball cap to shield his head from the Nevada sun. By 2035, AI and automation could put up to 92,000 Southern Nevada hospitality jobs at risk, or roughly one-third of that workforce, according to an analysis by RCG Economics.   Teamsters Local 986 has already been losing call-center workers at casinos to AI automation, while taxi drivers and valets face pressure from the expansion of autonomous-vehicle fleets operated by Waymo and Zoox. Robot bartenders and touchscreen hotel check-ins have also become increasingly common.   MGM Resorts laid off around 200 call-center workers last year, Kinson said. On a recent investor call, MGM International CFO Jonathan Halkyard said about 80 per cent of guest interactions "now take place via AI/digital platforms." MGM declined to comment for this story but directed Reuters to a labor contract it had reached with culinary union members in 2023. It promised advanced notice of AI-driven job losses along with health care and severance pay for those affected. The Las Vegas economy is no stranger to booms, busts and technological change. But how it navigates the AI-era will have huge consequences, said John Restrepo, principal of RCG Economics. "If they use those tools to just do massive job displacement, that's not going to be good," he said. Goldfinger said he worries the rise of AI in Las Vegas will not only cost the city lots of jobs, but also ultimately hurt business by making it less welcoming to tourists accustomed to interacting with well-trained hospitality staff.  "We are not against the changes," he said. "We just want to make sure we are involved in how it's changing." NEW GOLD RUSH   Every morning, Christopher Williams joins the traffic along the USA Parkway in northern Nevada's high desert on his way to an expanding cluster of data centers owned by Google, Switch, Tract and others in the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center.  The historic mining region was the site of a 19th-century gold rush, briefly earning Storey County the label of "the richest place on earth." Williams, a 20-year-old with curly black hair and glasses, is part of the new rush, this time for high-paying data-center jobs.  He moved from northern California to Reno last year after struggling to get enough hours as a line cook earning $18.50 an hour. Now he’s making more than $22 an hour and works 45 to 60 hours a week.  "I might not fully agree with data centers being built everywhere, but they are helping a lot of people," he said. "If I don't take the job, somebody else will, and it's a lot of money left on the table."  For local officials, the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center has been a lifeline after a prolonged economic slump.  "We're finding that our economy is more stable than it used to be as a primarily gaming and tourism economy, and it's providing opportunities, especially for young people that want to stay," said County Commissioner Clay Mitchell.  According to the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center has generated 850,000 work hours per month in 2026 – up from about the same number during all of 2022. BABY AND THE BATHWATER  The Nevada Teamsters’ internal discussions have led it to endorse Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford for governor, Kinson said.   Ford, who is seeking to unseat Republican incumbent Governor Joe Lombardo, has proposed halting new data-center tax abatements and requiring developers to shield residents from higher energy costs, and also wants strong regulation protecting jobs from AI - the right balance to appeal to the spectrum of Teamsters unions, Kinson said.  Ford had consulted with the Teamsters before launching his data-center platform this summer and hosted his first town hall about the issue at the Teamsters Local 14. Lombardo has championed data centers as a major economic driver, calling the industry a "new gold rush", but had been slower to embrace checks and balances on the industry, according to Kinson.  In September, Lombardo imposed new restrictions on some of the generous tax incentives that lured the industry to the state.  Lombardo did not respond to requests for comment.   The union’s influence tends to be significant. In 2025, union members accounted for about 13 per cent of wage and salary workers in Nevada, compared to 10 per cent nationwide, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.   In other parts of the United States, the data-center issue has also been key to union endorsement decisions.  In Kansas, for example, Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson won backing from the state's largest transit and railroad union, as well as from a local chapter of the IBEW electrical workers union, after Democratic rival Cindy Holscher called for a moratorium on data-center development.   It marked the first time in more than 50 years that the Kansas transit union backed a Republican candidate for governor.   Sean McGarvey, president of North America's Building Trades Unions, said – just like in Nevada – there is a division in the wider labor community around AI and data centers. But banning new data centers, he said, will never get their support.  "We don't throw the baby out with the bathwater," he said. "This is one of those once-in-a-lifetime opportunities to reindustrialize the country."

TOKYO, Oct 28 : A battle between private equity firms EQT and Bain to acquire a $5 billion Japanese internet company illustrates how takeovers in Japan are becoming increasingly contested, with the participation of strategic buyers helping push up prices. EQT bid for Kakaku.com in May, only for Bain to team up with SoftBank Group subsidiary LY Corp and submit a rival offer. That sparked a six-month bidding war in which EQT has hiked its offer price seven times to try to secure the support of Kakaku shareholders. It is the highest-profile takeover battle since KKR fended off Bain last year to buy Fuji Soft in a deal valuing the software firm at $4.1 billion, as private equity firms face off in a country relatively unused to contentious takeover battles. As more funds are taking more companies private, prospective buyers are factoring in the risk of battles and rising prices, dealmakers said. The trend of private equity firms working with non-financial firms, like Bain and LY, is also pushing up prices, they said.

Financial sponsor-backed M&A deals in Japan totalled $24 billion in January-September, just shy of a year earlier but almost double the $13 billion in the same period of 2024, LSEG data showed. Other contested deals include CVC and KKR's bid for cosmetics firm Mandom, and on Tuesday the Nikkei reported that Advantage Partners has countered Integral with a bid for Kadoya Sesame Mills. In the battle for Kakaku, EQT extended its offer period for the 10th time on Wednesday, with the deadline for shareholders to tender at the latest price of 3,683 yen ($23) a share on November 12. Bain and LY raised their offer to 3,700 yen on Monday, rising to 3,720 if they secure the support of Kakaku's third-largest shareholder KDDI. Kakaku's shares ended trading at 3,747 yen on Wednesday, indicating that market participants think further price hikes are possible. STRATEGIC COMPANIES SEE SYNERGY  Companies operating in the same sector as buyout targets may see more growth potential in the targets than funds acting alone so the idea of bidding together is gaining traction, said Yusuke Watanabe, a partner at private equity firm Carlyle. This trend is likely to push up the price of final bids, he said. LY, which operates the Line messaging app and Yahoo Japan internet portal, considered bidding for Kakaku in recent years, a person familiar with the matter said. When the media reported EQT's interest in April, LY decided to join Bain and make a counteroffer, the person said, declining to be identified as deliberations were private. LY has said it sees synergies between its internet businesses and Kakaku's price comparison website Kakaku.com and restaurant review website Tabelog.com. Such synergies include referring customers to LY's online services and integrating them into the payments ecosystem of SoftBank's digital wallet PayPay. In a similar case last month, telecommunications firm Hikari Tsushin joined forces with private equity firm MBK Partners and NEC Capital Solutions to buy Leopalace21, aiming to provide internet, gas and electricity to Leopalace's managed rental properties. Bringing in a strategic buyer also offers an exit option when funds struggle to offload investments, said Gregory Salathé, a partner at Freshfields law firm. EXPECTING MULTIPLE BIDDERS Such is the expectation for multiple bidders that a target is likely to consider auctioning itself rather than negotiating with a suitor, as was previously the norm, said Akihiko Manaka, co-head of investment banking and co-head of M&A in Japan at Bank of America. "If it's a good asset, the sort of company everyone wants, competition is naturally fierce, making it difficult to buy cheaply," Manaka said. "The buyers really have to work for it." ($1 = 157.4700 yen)

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Swiss banking software firm Temenos' CEO Takis Spiliopoulos said sovereign AI and cloud initiatives in Europe were not yet mature enough for major banks to adopt, as the region seeks greater technological autonomy from US providers. The European Union is seeking to strengthen its technological sovereignty through proposals, including the Cloud and AI Development Act, aimed at reducing dependence on US hyperscalers amid concerns over data access under US legislation and the dominance of Amazon, Microsoft and Google in cloud computing. • Spiliopoulos told Reuters that while many countries had pushed US cloud providers to establish local data centres, concerns remained over where data could ultimately be accessed. • "Sovereign data or sovereign AI ... it's not yet at a maturity level that they would really entertain this," Spiliopoulos said, referring to banks.

BANGKOK, Oct 28 : Thailand's central bank kept its key interest rate unchanged for a fourth straight meeting on Wednesday, as widely expected. The Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee voted unanimously to maintain the one-day repurchase rate at 1.00 per cent. All 26 economists polled by Reuters had expected the policy rate to remain unchanged.  "The monetary committee sees that low rates will have a long-term effect. If the economy is strong enough, rates can gradually rise to maintain policy space," Assistant Governor Don Nakornthab told a briefing Its next rate meeting is on December 23. The baht was largely unchanged after the decision.

The central bank forecast the economy would grow 2.4 per cent this year and 2.1 per cent in 2027, compared with its June forecasts of 2.3 per cent and 1.8 per cent, respectively, supported by stronger momentum in exports, plus technology and AI-related private investment.  "Nevertheless, overall growth remains below potential and the benefits remain concentrated," it said. Southeast Asia's second-largest economy expanded 1.9 per cent annually in the second quarter, down sharply from 2.8 per cent in the previous quarter. Last year's growth was 2.4 per cent and lagged regional peers.  RATE EXPECTED TO HOLD UNTIL END-2027 While many central banks including the Philippines have raised interest rates in response to inflationary pressures linked to the war in the Middle East, Thailand has kept its policy rate unchanged since the conflict started. Most economists polled by Reuters expect the rate to remain that way through to the end of 2027.  The central bank had cut the policy rate six times, by a total of 150 basis points, between October 2024 and February 2026 to support an economy constrained by sluggish domestic demand and high household debt. In an interview earlier this month, Deputy Governor Piti Disyatat said monetary policy would remain accommodative for now and the policy rate would normalise only when the economy was ready. The central bank now forecasts headline inflation at 2.1 per cent this year, compared with 2.2 per cent projected earlier this month. For 2027, it expects headline inflation at 1.3 per cent versus 1.4 per cent seen in June.       Exports, a key source of Thailand's growth, will rise 22 per cent this year, the BOT said, compared with a rise of 17 per cent to 18 per cent projected earlier this month and 14 per cent seen in June. It forecast export growth of 15 per cent in 2027 versus a rise of 4.6 per cent seen in June.  Foreign tourist arrivals, another key driver, are seen at 32 million this year and 34.5 million in 2027, the BOT said, both down by one million from previous forecasts.

By Anton Bridge TOKYO, Oct 28 : Nomura Holdings, Japan's largest brokerage and investment bank, said on Wednesday that its second-quarter net profit rose 13 per cent to 103.7 billion yen ($656.7 million), driven by steady growth in wealth management.  Its wholesale division's revenue grew 11 per cent from a year earlier, boosted by equity trading and investment banking.

The trading results mirrored other global investment banks, where strong trading in equities offset a fall in fixed income as bond yields spiked during the quarter. Fixed-income trading revenue fell 2 per cent from a year earlier, while revenue from equities rose 19 per cent. However, the results declined from the previous quarter, during which investor excitement over AI pushed stock markets in the US and Japan to record highs, helping to swell equity trading revenue. “The first quarter was extremely strong, so this quarter’s results are a bit of a normalization,” Nomura Chief Financial Officer Hiroyuki Moriuchi said.  Nomura has been a major beneficiary of Japanese firms' more active fundraising efforts as they seek growth opportunities amid rising domestic inflation. Nomura topped both equity capital markets and debt capital markets league tables in Japan over the six months to the end of September, with revenue buoyed by the take-private move of Dentsu Research Institute and SoftBank Group's record 1 trillion yen retail bond issuance. The wholesale division has had a slower start to the third quarter, but its investment banking pipeline remains healthy, Moriuchi said. While favourable market conditions have lifted profit over the past year, Nomura's wealth management division continued to grow as Japanese households steadily move away from cash and deposits toward higher-yielding investments. Nomura has sought for a number of years to develop steady sources of revenue that are less impacted by market volatility and the wealth management division's recurring revenue reached a record high of 66.7 billion yen, up 30 per cent from a year earlier.
